simple: a whole small computer on one chip: processor, program memory, working memory and helpers for the outside world.
analogy: the take-away kitchen in one room.
precise: an integrated circuit that combines one or more processor cores with on-chip non-volatile program memory (usually flash), on-chip SRAM, a bus system and memory-mapped peripherals such as timers, serial ports and general-purpose I/O, designed to run one program directly on the hardware or under a small real-time OS.
source: D2, D3 of F1-73 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small machine on the chip that does one job, such as counting time or sending characters.
analogy: the kitchen timer, the hot plate, the order window.
precise: a hardware block on the chip, controlled by reading and writing its registers at fixed addresses (memory-mapped I/O, F1-41).
source: D4, D3 of F1-73 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: memory that keeps the program when the power is off.
analogy: the laminated recipe book screwed to the wall.
precise: non-volatile memory on the chip from which the core fetches instructions and constant data; it is read like memory but written only through a special programming procedure. (Flash is the subject of F1-74.)
source: D2 of F1-73 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the chip's small working memory, which forgets everything when power goes.
analogy: the counter top.
precise: static RAM on the chip holding variables, the stack and any heap; its contents are undefined after power-up unless start-up code writes them.
source: D2, D7 of F1-73 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a list of addresses at a fixed place that tells the core where to start and where to go for each kind of event.
analogy: the first page of the recipe book: "stand here, start with recipe 1, if the doorbell rings go to recipe 5".
precise: on Armv7-M, a table of 32-bit words whose word 0 is the initial main stack pointer value and whose word 1 is the address of the reset handler, followed by the addresses of the handlers of the other exceptions and interrupts.
source: D1, R1 of F1-73 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the first function that runs after power-on or reset.
analogy: recipe 1, the morning routine before any customer arrives.
precise: the code whose address is in vector-table word 1; it prepares memory for the language (copies .data, clears .bss, runs constructors if any) and calls main.
source: D1, D2 of F1-73 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the small program, written by you or your vendor, that sets the chip up before main.
analogy: opening the stand: lights, counter wiped, first ingredients out.
precise: the vector table plus the reset handler and default exception handlers, together with the linker-script symbols they rely on.
source: D2, C1 of F1-73 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a text file that tells the linker which memory exists and where each part of the program goes.
analogy: the floor plan saying which shelf holds what.
precise: input to the linker (GNU ld, LLD) with a MEMORY command describing regions and a SECTIONS command placing input sections into output sections at addresses in those regions, and defining symbols.
source: D9 of F1-73 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: C++ with no operating system and almost no library underneath.
analogy: cooking without a manager or a supplier: you bring every tool yourself.
precise: a C++ implementation kind in which only a small set of headers is required and program start-up is implementation-defined; firmware is built this way (here with -ffreestanding -nostdlib -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti).
source: D7, R1 of F1-73 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: your program runs directly on the chip with nothing else below it.
analogy: the cook is also the manager.
precise: firmware that runs without an operating system or RTOS and owns all of the hardware, from the reset handler on (contrast with an RTOS or Linux in BR-05).
source: D3, C1 of F1-73 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of which address ranges hold which memory or device.
analogy: the plan of the room on the napkin.
precise: the assignment of the processor's physical address space to on-chip flash, SRAM, peripheral register blocks, the core's private peripherals and unused (reserved) ranges, as documented in the chip's reference manual and datasheet.
source: D2, D1 of F1-74 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a named block of a compiled program, such as "all the code" or "all the zeroed variables".
analogy: the labelled boxes the supplier delivers: recipes, spices, empty jars.
precise: a contiguous part of an object or executable file with a name, flags and alignment; compilers put code in .text, constants in .rodata, initialised variables in .data and zero-initialised variables in .bss.
source: D3, D4 of F1-74 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the address where a part of the program is when the program runs.
analogy: the sauce recipe's place on the counter.
precise: virtual memory address of an output section: the address the code uses to access it at run time. On a microcontroller without an MMU it is a physical address.
source: D3 of F1-74 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the address where that part is stored in the image that gets flashed.
analogy: the sauce recipe's page in the book.
precise: load memory address of an output section: where its contents are placed in the loaded image; it differs from the VMA when start-up code must copy the section, as for .data.
source: D3, R2 of F1-74 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the linker's report of where it put everything.
analogy: the delivery note listing which box went on which shelf.
precise: a text file written by the linker (option -Map) listing each output section, its VMA, LMA, size and alignment, the input sections it contains and the symbols defined in them.
source: D3, R2 of F1-74 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the same memory seen at two different addresses.
analogy: the recipe book has a copy of its first pages hanging by the door.
precise: an address range that decodes to the same physical memory as another range; many microcontrollers make flash (or a boot ROM, or SRAM, chosen at boot) visible at address 0 as well as at its own address.
source: D2, R1 of F1-74 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the linker throws away parts of the program that nothing uses.
analogy: head office removes pages nobody refers to from the recipe book.
precise: with --gc-sections, the linker removes input sections not reachable from the entry symbol or from sections marked KEEP in the linker script.
source: D3, R4 of F1-74 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the set of control knobs and display windows of one peripheral, each at its own address.
analogy: an appliance's control panel.
precise: a contiguous range of memory-mapped registers belonging to one peripheral instance, at a base address plus fixed offsets, each register with documented fields, reset value and access type.
source: D1, D3 of F1-75 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what you are allowed to do with a register bit: read it, write it, or clear it by writing a 1.
analogy: a dial you can turn, a lamp you can only look at, a "reset" button.
precise: the documented behaviour of a field on read and write, such as read-write, read-only, write-only, or write-1-to-clear; reference manuals use short codes for these (F1-78).
source: D1 of F1-75 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the network that takes one or two basic ticking signals and makes all the speeds the chip's parts need.
analogy: the stand's rhythm, passed on and slowed down for each helper.
precise: the oscillators, phase-locked loops, multiplexers, dividers (prescalers) and gates that generate and distribute the clock signals of a chip, from the clock sources to each bus and peripheral.
source: D1, D2 of F1-75 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part that produces the basic tick.
analogy: the first beat Amara taps.
precise: a clock source; an on-chip RC oscillator needs no external parts but is less accurate, while a crystal oscillator uses an external quartz crystal for an accurate frequency.
source: D2, D4 of F1-75 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a circuit that makes a faster clock from a slower one.
analogy: the second cook joins and the beat doubles.
precise: a feedback circuit that locks an internal oscillator to a multiple of its reference input; on microcontrollers it multiplies an oscillator's frequency to produce the high system clock.
source: D2, D4 of F1-75 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a divider that slows a clock down by a fixed number.
analogy: "move at every second beat".
precise: a frequency divider in the clock path, set by a register field, producing fout = fin / N.
source: D1 of F1-75 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: switching a peripheral's clock on or off with one bit.
analogy: the appliance's wall switch.
precise: a gate in a peripheral's clock path controlled by an enable bit in the clock controller; with the clock off, the peripheral's logic does not change state, which saves power, and on many chips its registers cannot be written.
source: D1, D2 of F1-75 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many symbols per second a serial line sends, and the number that sets it.
analogy: how fast ticket numbers are called.
precise: the symbol rate of a UART; the peripheral derives it from its input clock through a programmable divisor, so the divisor must be computed from the peripheral clock actually present.
source: D3, D1 of F1-75 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a pin the program can switch on and off, or read as on or off.
analogy: the lamp switch over the order window, and the bell button customers press.
precise: a pin whose direction, output level and input sampling are controlled by software through the GPIO peripheral's registers (direction or mode, output data, input data, and often pull-up/pull-down and output-type settings).
source: D1, D2 of F1-76 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two ways a pin can drive a wire: actively high and low, or only pulling low.
analogy: a door you can push and pull, versus one you can only pull shut while a spring opens it.
precise: a push-pull output has transistors to both supply and ground and drives either level; an open-drain output has only the transistor to ground, so the high level must come from a pull-up resistor, which lets several outputs share one wire (as I2C does).
source: D3, D1 of F1-76 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a weak connection that keeps an unconnected input at a defined level.
analogy: a spring that holds a door shut until someone pushes.
precise: a resistor (internal, enabled by a GPIO register, or external on the board) from an input to the supply or to ground, so that the input reads a known value when nothing drives it.
source: D3 of F1-76 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a counter that counts clock ticks by itself and raises a flag when it reaches a set value.
analogy: the kitchen timer that rings at a steady beat.
precise: a peripheral with a counter register clocked by a (prescaled) peripheral clock, a reload or compare value that defines its period, a status flag set at each period, and usually an interrupt request and compare/capture channels.
source: D1, D4 of F1-76 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number the timer counts to (or from) before starting again.
analogy: how many seconds the kitchen timer is set to.
precise: the register whose value defines the counter's period; for a counter running 0…N or N…0 the period is N + 1 counter clocks.
source: D1, R2 of F1-76 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: switching a pin on and off very fast with a chosen fraction of "on" time.
analogy: flicking the lamp so fast it looks dimmer.
precise: a periodic digital signal whose period is fixed and whose high time (pulse width) encodes a value; the ratio of high time to period is the duty cycle.
source: D4, D3 of F1-76 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much of each cycle the signal is on, in percent.
analogy: a quarter of each moment on = 25 %.
precise: high time divided by period; for an edge-aligned PWM with compare value C and period N + 1 counts, duty = C / (N + 1).
source: R1 of F1-76 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a second number the timer watches, used to switch an output in the middle of each period.
analogy: a mark on the kitchen timer's dial: "switch the lamp off here".
precise: a register compared with the counter on every count; the comparison drives an output pin in PWM modes or raises an event flag.
source: D1 of F1-76 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small box between your computer's USB port and the chip's debug pins.
analogy: the inspector's hand on the pause button.
precise: an adapter that translates debugger requests (halt, read register, write memory, set breakpoint) from the host into JTAG or SWD transactions on the target's debug port; usually paired with host software that acts as a GDB server.
source: D2, D3 of F1-77 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an old, standard four- or five-wire interface for testing and debugging chips.
analogy: a hatch with a strict door protocol: knock patterns move you from room to room.
precise: the IEEE 1149.1 test access port and boundary-scan architecture: signals TCK (clock), TMS (mode select), TDI (data in), TDO (data out) and optional TRST, a 16-state TAP controller driven by TMS, an instruction register and several data registers shifted serially.
source: D1 of F1-77 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the little state machine behind the JTAG pins.
analogy: the corridor map of the inspection rooms.
precise: a 16-state finite-state machine advanced on each TCK rising edge by the value of TMS, which selects whether an instruction or a data register is captured, shifted between TDI and TDO, and updated.
source: D1, R1 of F1-77 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: Arm's two-wire replacement for JTAG on small chips.
analogy: the same hatch with a smaller door.
precise: a two-pin (SWDIO bidirectional data, SWCLK clock) packet protocol defined by the Arm Debug Interface architecture; each transaction is a request, an acknowledgement and a 32-bit data phase with parity, addressed to debug-port or access-port registers.
source: D2, D3 of F1-77 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the doorway inside the chip that turns probe packets into memory reads and writes.
analogy: the inspector's assistant inside the kitchen who fetches what she asks for.
precise: in the Arm Debug Interface, the debug port (JTAG-DP or SW-DP) is the external interface, and access ports behind it, such as a memory access port, perform bus transactions on the chip's memory system, including the core's debug registers.
source: D3 of F1-77 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "stop when the program reaches this instruction".
analogy: "freeze when the cook opens recipe 15".
precise: a software breakpoint replaces an instruction with a breakpoint instruction (bkpt on Arm), which needs writable code memory; a hardware breakpoint is an address comparator in the core's debug logic (on Armv7-M, the Flash Patch and Breakpoint unit), which works on flash but exists in limited number.
source: D4, D2 of F1-77 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "stop when this memory location is read or written".
analogy: "freeze when anyone touches the salt jar".
precise: a data-address comparator (on Armv7-M, in the Data Watchpoint and Trace unit) that halts the core after a matching access; the stop is reported at the instruction after the access.
source: D4, R2 of F1-77 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the text protocol a debugger uses to talk to a stub that controls the target.
analogy: the phone line from the inspector's office to her hand on the button.
precise: a packet protocol (read registers, read/write memory, insert breakpoint, continue, stop reply) spoken by GDB and LLDB; probe software and QEMU's -gdb option implement the server side.
source: D5, D6 of F1-77 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a default definition that is silently replaced if someone defines the same name.
analogy: a "standard recipe" card that is used unless the cook pins a card with exactly the same title.
precise: a symbol marked weak (GCC/Clang __attribute__((weak))) that the linker uses only if no strong definition of the same name exists; it is how start-up files provide default handlers.
source: D7, R3 of F1-77 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the short document about one chip: what is inside, its pins, its electrical limits.
analogy: the oven's leaflet.
precise: the per-part document giving features, pinout and package, absolute maximum ratings, operating conditions, electrical and timing characteristics and ordering codes; it rarely explains how to program peripherals.
source: D1, D2 of F1-78 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the thick document that explains every peripheral and every register of a chip family.
analogy: the oven's service manual.
precise: the family-level programming document containing the memory map, the clock/reset/power chapter and one chapter per peripheral (functional description and register descriptions); the core itself is described in a separate core or architecture manual.
source: D1, D3 of F1-78 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of things in the chip that do not work as the manuals say.
analogy: the "known issues" page.
precise: a vendor document listing silicon defects per device revision, each with its effect and a workaround; it overrides the reference manual for the revisions it names.
source: D1 of F1-78 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the table of all registers of one peripheral, with their positions.
analogy: the diagram of the oven's control panel.
precise: a table of register names, offsets from the peripheral's base address, reset values and (often) a bit-field summary; the absolute address is base + offset.
source: D3, R1 of F1-78 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what a register contains right after reset.
analogy: the knob positions the oven leaves the factory with.
precise: the value each bit takes on reset, given per register; firmware must not assume any other value, and "x" or "undefined" marks bits without one.
source: D3 of F1-78 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: bits you must leave alone.
analogy: the screws marked "service only".
precise: bits without a documented function; manuals specify how to write them (typically "keep at reset value" or "write 0"), which is why firmware uses read-modify-write or writes complete documented values.
source: D3, R1 of F1-78 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a flag you clear by writing 1 to it, not 0.
analogy: a "done" lamp you switch off by pressing it.
precise: an access type in which writing 1 to a bit clears it and writing 0 has no effect; it lets software clear one flag without disturbing others set by hardware meanwhile. Other manuals use read-to-clear or write-0-to-clear for similar flags: the access column decides.
source: D3, R1 of F1-78 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a register whose new value takes effect later, not at the moment you write it.
analogy: "the new temperature applies from the next baking cycle".
precise: a register with a preload copy that software writes and an active copy that the hardware uses; the preload is transferred to the active copy at a defined event (for a timer, the update event), so that changes never take effect in the middle of a period.
source: D3, R1 of F1-78 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the moment a timer restarts its count and takes on new settings.
analogy: the start of a new baking cycle.
precise: in the teaching chip's TIM2 (and many real timers), the event generated when the counter wraps or when software sets the update-generation bit; it reloads buffered registers and sets the update flag.
source: R1 of F1-78 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a drawing of which parts of a circuit are connected to which, using symbols.
analogy: the stand's wiring plan.
precise: a diagram of a circuit's components (as standard symbols with reference designators and values) and their electrical connections (wires, net labels, power symbols); it shows connectivity, not physical layout.
source: D1, D2 of F1-79 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the schematic written as a list of "this pin connects to that wire".
analogy: the electrician's cable list.
precise: a text description of a circuit's components and the nets each terminal is connected to, exported by schematic-capture tools and used for layout and checking.
source: D2, R1 of F1-79 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one electrical connection, and the name written on it.
analogy: one cable, with its tag.
precise: a net is a set of terminals that are electrically the same node; a net label gives it a name, and two wires with the same label are connected even if no line is drawn between them.
source: D2 of F1-79 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the short name of each part on a board, like R1 or U1.
analogy: the numbered tag on each appliance.
precise: a unique identifier made of a letter prefix for the part type (R resistor, C capacitor, D diode/LED, U integrated circuit, SW switch, J connector) and a number, linking schematic, bill of materials and the printed board.
source: D1 of F1-79 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: limits that may damage the chip if exceeded, even briefly.
analogy: "never above 250 °C" on the oven: not a cooking temperature.
precise: the datasheet table of stress limits (supply voltage, pin voltages, pin and total currents, temperatures) beyond which permanent damage may occur; operation is guaranteed only within the separate, narrower operating conditions.
source: D1, D3 of F1-79 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the tables saying what the chip guarantees under normal conditions.
analogy: the rating plate's normal values.
precise: datasheet tables of parameters (output voltage at a given current, input thresholds, leakage, pull-up resistance, supply current) with minimum, typical and maximum values under stated conditions; designs must use min/max, because typical values are not guaranteed.
source: D1, D3 of F1-79 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small capacitor next to a chip's power pin that smooths its supply.
analogy: a small water tank next to the tap for sudden demand.
precise: a capacitor (often 100 nF ceramic per supply pin, plus bulk capacitance) placed close to an IC's supply and ground pins to supply fast current transients and reduce supply noise; datasheets specify the arrangement.
source: D1, D3 of F1-79 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a part that is drawn in the schematic but not soldered on the board.
analogy: a socket drawn on the plan but never installed.
precise: a marking on a schematic or bill of materials for footprints left empty in a given build variant; firmware must treat the part as absent.
source: D2 of F1-79 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: whether "on" means the pin is high or low.
analogy: a switch that is "on" when up, versus one that is "on" when down.
precise: a signal is active-high if its asserted state is the high voltage level and active-low if it is the low level; an LED from pin to ground is active-high, an LED from supply to pin is active-low, a button to ground with a pull-up reads low when pressed.
source: D1, R1 of F1-79 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the short document that tells a programmer everything about one board.
analogy: the stand's handbook for a new cook.
precise: in this course, a document collecting a board's chip and document revisions, memory map and linker settings, clock configuration, pin assignments with active levels, start-up and build commands, debug connection, bring-up evidence and known issues, each with its verification status.
source: C1 of F1-79 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)
